conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in with right upper abdominal pain and a fever—can you tell me more about what happened today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain started around 3 p.m. It’s in the upper right side, and it spreads a bit across the middle. I felt nauseous but didn’t throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever? Chills? Changes in your urine or stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a low fever earlier, up to 100.4. No chills. Urine seems normal. I’ve had diarrhea for a few weeks now—started after I began doxycycline last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We know you have primary sclerosing cholangitis and cirrhosis. This sounds like a flare-up—possibly cholangitis again. We gave you antibiotics in the ER—meropenem—and some pain and nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. The morphine helped the pain a little. Is this serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we take seriously, but you’re stable. Your labs show elevated liver enzymes, but no infection markers in the blood yet. No sign of kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been through this before. Last time, I was on meropenem too. But why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your PSC, bile flow can get blocked or slowed. You have a small stone in the right hepatic duct—seen on ultrasound. It hasn’t changed, but it could still cause inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So will they remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering an ERCP—a scope procedure—to look inside the ducts. If there’s a blockage or stricture, we might treat it. But we’ll wait for more imaging review first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your fever went up to 101.7 when you arrived, but it’s down now. Your repeat labs show liver enzymes are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. We’re continuing meropenem every six hours. The team reviewed your ultrasound again—there may be a subtle stricture upstream, so we’re scheduling an ERCP for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they take a biopsy during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If they see anything suspicious, they’ll take a small sample. But the main goal is to check for blockages and clear them if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the diarrhea? Is it from the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool for C. diff—it came back negative. So it’s likely a side effect. We’ll stop doxycycline and switch your prevention plan after this episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from ERCP. The good news: no stones or strictures that needed treatment. They took a small biopsy from the duct, but everything looked stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing was blocking the duct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The ducts were narrow in places, which is expected with PSC, but nothing that could be opened today. The antibiotics are doing the job—your pain and fever are gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Do I still need IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’ll make it easier. We’re placing a PICC line today so you can finish a five-day course of ertapenem at home—just once a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A line in my arm? Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s common. A small tube goes into a vein in your arm, and we’ll confirm placement with an X-ray. It lets you get antibiotics at home without daily needles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line is in—placed in your right arm. The chest X-ray confirms it’s positioned well, though it’s a bit too far in. We’ll pull it back slightly to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? How do I care for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some pressure, but no sharp pain. A nurse will teach you how to keep it clean and what signs of infection to watch for—redness, swelling, fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look good. White count is low but stable, liver enzymes are nearly normal. You’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart all your usual meds—ursodiol, furosemide, levothyroxine, omeprazole, and lisinopril. We’re adding rifaximin after you finish the IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does rifaximin do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an antibiotic that stays in the gut. It helps reduce bacteria that can trigger cholangitis in people with PSC, and it’s less likely to cause diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better than doxycycline. Should I still follow up with my gastroenterologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. You’re due for a colonoscopy too, since you have PSC and a history of possible Crohn’s. Your GI doctor will help schedule that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your discharge plan. You’ll get five more days of ertapenem through the PICC line, then start rifaximin twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC line—when does it come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After your last dose, a home health nurse will remove it. They’ll also check the site and give you instructions for care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Just keep an eye on your temperature, the PICC site, and let someone know if the pain comes back or you feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray after the PICC adjustment looks good—line is now in the right spot. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll leave in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. I’ll start the new plan and follow up with my GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you only if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really well. Pain is gone, no fever. I’m eating normally again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam confirms that—abdomen soft, only mild tenderness. You’re cleared to go home with services for IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.
